explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, covenant. God says, “I will establish My covenant between Me and you…” A covenant is a binding promise, and this one comes straight from God Almighty. Abram is ninety-nine and just got handed a promise bigger than his whole tent.

Temple is a fair guess, since it sounds holy. But no temple comes up in this talk. God says, “I will establish My covenant between Me and you…” What He's building here is a promise between Him and Abram.

A throne sounds big and important, and I respect that. But God never says throne here. He says, “I will establish My covenant between Me and you…” It's a promise, and Abram doesn't even need to sit down for it. He ends up facedown, actually.

That's it. God says, “You will be the father of many nations.” Abram is ninety-nine, and God is talking about a family tree with a lot of branches. That's a big promise to hear from a man's own front yard.

An army is a strong guess, but God doesn't say it. He tells Abram, “You will be the father of many nations.” Nations are whole peoples, not just soldiers. God's promise is bigger than a battle lineup.
A royal city would be nice, and Abram could use a good address. But God doesn't promise one here. He says, “You will be the father of many nations.” This promise is about people, not buildings.

Yes! God says, “No longer will you be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations.” So the new name comes with the promise. Every time somebody says Abraham, the promise gets said too.

Israel is a name you'll hear later in this story, so I see why it came to mind. But here God says, “…your name will be Abraham…” Israel is the name God later gives Abraham's grandson Jacob (Genesis 32:28). That's down the road, friend.

Judah shows up later in the family, but not here. God says, “…your name will be Abraham…” Judah is one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:23), and Jacob is Abraham's grandson (Genesis 25:19, 26). So Judah is a few generations away from this conversation.
That's right. God says, “I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you.” Nations and kings in the same breath. Abraham came for a talk and left with a whole royal family tree.

Prophets are a good guess, and they do show up in the Bible later. But in this verse God says, “I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you.” Kings is the word He picks. We stay with what He actually says.

Judges is a fair guess, but it's not the word God uses. He says, “I will make nations of you, and kings will descend from you.” So the promise here is kings. I'd sure be nervous about the guest list at that family reunion.

True. God says, “I will establish My covenant as an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you…” Everlasting means it isn't a one-batch deal. It reaches Abraham's family down the line, and God says He will be their God too.

It's actually true. God says, “I will establish My covenant as an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you…” He's not talking about a promise with an expiration date. It's meant for Abraham and the family coming after him.

Canaan is it. God says, “…I will give the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan—as an eternal possession…” Abraham is living there right now as a resident. God is saying it'll belong to his family for good.

Egypt is in this story, since Hagar, Sarai's maidservant, was an Egyptian (Genesis 16:1). But God doesn't promise Egypt here. He says, “…the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan…” The land He gives is the one under Abraham's feet.

Moab is a fun name, but it's not the land God names here. He says, “…the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan…” Think of the place Abraham is standing as he hears it. That's the one God promises.
Yes. God says, “Every male among you must be circumcised.” That's the part Abraham and his family keep. God makes the covenant promise, and this is how they show they belong to it.
Offering a lamb is a good guess, but it's not what God asks here. He says, “Every male among you must be circumcised.” That's the instruction in this conversation. Keep your eyes on that one.

The Sabbath is a real thing in Scripture, but God doesn't bring it up in this talk with Abraham. Here He says, “Every male among you must be circumcised.” That's the part Abraham's family is asked to keep. One instruction at a time, friend.

True. God says, “You are to circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you.” A sign is something you can see. This one marks every male in the covenant family.
It's actually true. God says, “…this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you.” He calls it a sign, a mark that points to the promise. So it's not random. It means something.

It's false, and I can see how it slips by. God says every male must be circumcised, “including those born in your household and those purchased from a foreigner…” Then He says it again: “Whether they are born in your household or purchased, they must be circumcised.” No loopholes here, friend.

That's right, it's false. God says every male must be circumcised, “including those born in your household and those purchased from a foreigner—even those who are not your offspring.” Then He repeats it in verse 13. Born in the household or bought, the covenant sign covers them.

explanations.answer: He will be cut off from his people
explanations.explanation: That's what God says: “…he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant.” The text puts those two things together right there. God treats this as a serious matter, so we keep it serious too.

explanations.answer: He will have to pay a fine
explanations.explanation: A fine sounds reasonable, like a late fee at the library. But God doesn't mention one. He says, “…he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant.” That's the consequence the text gives.

explanations.answer: He will have to fast seven days
explanations.explanation: Fasting seven days is a creative guess, I'll give you that. But God doesn't say anything about fasting here. He says, “…he will be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant.” We stay with His words.
A son, yes. God says, “I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her.” Sarah is Abraham's wife, and the promise runs through her. Notice the word “surely.” God isn't hedging.

A daughter would be a lovely gift, but that's not what God says. He tells Abraham, “I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her.” Sarah is Abraham's wife, and the promise is a son. The word “surely” sits right in the verse.

Abraham already has a big household, so servants are a natural guess. But God says, “I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her.” This promise is about a child, not staff. God is talking about family here.
True. God says Sarah “will be the mother of nations; kings of peoples will descend from her.” Sarah gets a new name and a promise to match. She's not a bystander in this covenant.

It's actually true. God says, “I will bless her and will surely give you a son by her… she will be the mother of nations; kings of peoples will descend from her.” That's God's own word about Sarah. She's right in the middle of this promise.

explanations.answer: If a man of a hundred can have a child
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Abraham says to himself, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” He laughs while he's down on the ground. I think he's trying to wrap his head around it, and honestly, so would I.

explanations.answer: Why God waited so long to speak to him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give Abraham that question. What he says to himself is, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” He's asking about a child, and his own age is part of it. That's what the verse shows.

explanations.answer: Whether Ishmael will become a great king
explanations.explanation: Ishmael is on Abraham's mind, but not in this question. Ishmael is Abraham's son, and Abraham speaks up for him next, in verse 18. The question he asks himself while laughing is, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?”

explanations.answer: That he might live under God's blessing
explanations.explanation: Yes. Abraham says, “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!” Ishmael is Abraham's son, and Abraham wants good for him. I think that's a dad talking.

explanations.answer: That he might rule over the land of Canaan
explanations.explanation: Ruling Canaan isn't what Abraham asks. He says, “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!” The land of Canaan was promised to Abraham's descendants earlier in this talk (verse 8). Abraham's ask is about blessing.

explanations.answer: That he might stay in Abraham's household
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Abraham ask that. He says, “O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!” Ishmael is Abraham's son, and the request is for God's blessing on his life.
Isaac is right. God says, “Your wife Sarah will indeed bear you a son, and you are to name him Isaac.” God hands over the name before the baby is even on the way. That's a head start.
Jacob is a name from this family, but he comes later. He's Isaac's son and Abraham's grandson (Genesis 25:19, 26). The son God names here is Isaac: “…you are to name him Isaac.”
Joseph is a famous name in this family, but he's much later. He's Jacob's son (Genesis 37:3), so he's Abraham's great-grandson. God's instruction here is, “…you are to name him Isaac.”

Twelve is right. God says Ishmael “will become the father of twelve rulers, and I will make him into a great nation.” God answers Abraham's request with a promise to bless Ishmael, in His own words. That's a lot of family to feed.
Seven is a number the Bible loves, but it's not the one here. God says Ishmael “will become the father of twelve rulers…” So the promise is twelve rulers. Close, friend, but the count is higher.
Forty is a big number, but God doesn't say it here. He says Ishmael “will become the father of twelve rulers…” That's a lot of rulers already. No need to pad the count.

It's false, and I get why Ishmael's blessing might make it sound that way. But God says, “I will establish My covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this time next year.” God does bless Ishmael (verse 20). The covenant is with Isaac, though.

That's right, it's false. God says, “I will establish My covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this time next year.” He also says He has heard Abraham about Ishmael and will surely bless him (verse 20). Ishmael is blessed, and the covenant goes to Isaac.
Yes. God says Sarah will bear Isaac “at this time next year.” That's not a vague someday. Abraham gets a date on the calendar.
Seven years would be a long wait, but God doesn't say that. He says Sarah will bear Isaac “at this time next year.” One year is the timeline He gives. Abraham should start clearing space.
Ishmael is already thirteen (verse 25), so that's not a long way off. But God doesn't tie Isaac's birth to Ishmael growing up. He says Sarah will bear Isaac “at this time next year.”

That very day, yes. The text says, “On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael and all those born in his household or purchased with his money…” There's no sleeping on it and no putting it off. I've seen people take longer to answer a text message.

Eight days is in this passage, but for a different reason. It's the age for baby boys to be circumcised (verse 12). For Abraham, the text says, “On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael…” He doesn't wait.
Next year is when God says Isaac will be born (verse 21), so that's where the timing got mixed up. But Abraham doesn't wait for that. The text says, “On that very day Abraham took his son Ishmael…”

Male is right. Abraham circumcises Ishmael and “every male among the members of Abraham's household,” just as God had told him. He does what God said, to everyone God said. That's a full day of work, friend.

Firstborn is a good guess, but the text doesn't say that. It says Abraham circumcised “every male among the members of Abraham's household.” God's instruction wasn't limited to the oldest. Every male means every male.
Elder doesn't appear in this verse. The text says Abraham circumcised “every male among the members of Abraham's household.” That covers everyone from Ishmael to the servants, so no one gets skipped.
